config.title: Type Coercion, Equality & Truthy/Falsy

intro.title: Type Coercion, Equality & Truthy/Falsy
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple interactive program that demonstrates how JavaScript handles type coercion, equality comparisons, and truthy/falsy values. You will learn the core programming concepts of implicit and explicit type conversion, the difference between loose (==) and strict (===) equality, and what makes a value truthy or falsy in logical contexts. The main technologies involved are JavaScript's comparison operators, logical operators, and conditional statements. This hands-on practice will help you predict and control how your code behaves when different data types interact, a fundamental skill for debugging and writing robust JavaScript applications.
intro.usecase: Understanding type coercion, equality, and truthy/falsy values is essential for handling user input in web forms and interactive UI components. For example, when validating a login form, you might check if an email field is empty (falsy) or compare a user's age input (a string) to a minimum number (using loose equality). In a dashboard filter, you might use truthy checks to conditionally display data panels only when filters are applied. These concepts prevent bugs in dynamic features like search bars, modals, and data-driven menus where values can unexpectedly change types.

objectives: Apply type coercion rules to convert values between string, number, and boolean types
Construct equality comparisons using both strict (===) and loose (==) operators
Manipulate truthy and falsy values in conditional statements
Implement type checking and conversion functions for data validation
Configure logical operators to work with coerced boolean values
Integrate type coercion and equality concepts into practical JavaScript scenarios
Control variable behavior by applying explicit type conversion techniques

steps.title: Create a JavaScript file and define a main function
steps.instruction: Create a new JavaScript file (e.g., index.js) and define a main function named 'typeCoercionDemo' that will contain all the lesson code.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Make sure the function has a name and a body.
steps.expectedOutcome: A JavaScript file with a main function defined, ready to hold the lesson's code about type coercion, equality, and truthy/falsy values.
successCriteria: A function named 'typeCoercionDemo' is defined in the JavaScript file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've defined a function with the exact name 'typeCoercionDemo'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please create a function named 'typeCoercionDemo' to serve as the main entry point for this lesson.

steps.title: Initialize variables to demonstrate type coercion
steps.instruction: Inside the 'typeCoercionDemo' function, declare three variables: a string variable named 'strNum' with value '5', a number variable named 'num' with value 10, and a boolean variable named 'bool' with value true.
steps.hint: Use the 'let' keyword to declare each variable and assign the specified values. For example: let strNum = '5';
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will contain three variables with different data types that can be used to demonstrate type coercion in later steps.
successCriteria: The function contains variables named 'strNum' (string '5'), 'num' (number 10), and 'bool' (boolean true).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've declared some variables, but make sure you have all three: strNum (string '5'), num (number 10), and bool (boolean true).
steps.feedbackWrong: The variables aren't declared correctly. Inside the function, declare three variables: strNum = '5', num = 10, and bool = true.

steps.title: Demonstrate string concatenation with numbers
steps.instruction: Inside the typeCoercionDemo function, create two examples of string concatenation with numbers using the + operator. First, concatenate a string with a number. Second, concatenate a number with a string.
steps.hint: Use the + operator between a string (in quotes) and a number (without quotes). JavaScript will automatically convert the number to a string.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will contain two examples showing how JavaScript coerces numbers to strings during concatenation.
successCriteria: Two concatenation examples are created inside the function: one starting with a string and one starting with a number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both examples: one starting with a string and one starting with a number.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating two examples inside the function: one where a string is concatenated with a number, and one where a number is concatenated with a string.

steps.title: Demonstrate numeric operations with strings
steps.instruction: Inside the typeCoercionDemo function, add two examples where strings are used in subtraction operations to show JavaScript's numeric coercion.
steps.hint: Create variables that subtract string numbers, like '10' - '5', and subtract a string number from a regular number, like 20 - '5'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will now include examples demonstrating how JavaScript converts strings to numbers during subtraction operations.
successCriteria: Two subtraction examples are added inside the function: one subtracting two string numbers, and one subtracting a string number from a regular number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some numeric operation examples, but make sure to include both: subtracting two strings and subtracting a string from a number.
steps.feedbackWrong: The numeric operation examples are missing or incorrect. Add two subtraction examples inside the function to demonstrate type coercion.

steps.title: Compare values using strict equality (===)
steps.instruction: Inside your typeCoercionDemo function, add strict equality comparisons (===) for the same value pairs you used with loose equality to demonstrate the difference.
steps.hint: Use the === operator to compare values. This checks both value and type without coercion.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will include strict equality comparisons that return different results than loose equality comparisons for the same value pairs.
successCriteria: The typeCoercionDemo function contains at least one strict equality comparison (===) operation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the === operator for strict equality comparisons inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The strict equality comparisons aren't present. Remember to use === to compare values without type coercion.

steps.title: Create conditional checks using truthy/falsy values
steps.instruction: Inside the typeCoercionDemo function, write an if/else statement that checks a truthy value (like a non-empty string) and logs an appropriate message to the console.
steps.hint: You can use a variable that holds a truthy value (e.g., a string with text) directly in an if condition without comparing it to true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function will include a conditional statement that demonstrates how truthy values are evaluated directly in if conditions.
successCriteria: An if/else statement is added inside typeCoercionDemo that uses a truthy value (like a non-empty string) directly in the condition and logs a message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your if/else statement uses a truthy value (like a non-empty string) directly in the condition and logs a message to the console.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional check is missing or incorrect. Remember to write an if/else statement that uses a truthy value directly in the condition and logs a message.

steps.title: Build a demonstration function for equality comparisons
steps.instruction: Define a function named 'equalityDemo' that takes two parameters, compares them using both loose (==) and strict (===) equality, and returns an object with the comparison results.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts two parameters, performs both types of equality comparisons, and returns an object containing the results.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new function named 'equalityDemo' that demonstrates both loose and strict equality comparisons by returning an object with the results.
successCriteria: The 'equalityDemo' function is defined with two parameters, performs both == and === comparisons, and returns an object containing both results.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function takes two parameters, performs both == and === comparisons, and returns an object with both results.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function named 'equalityDemo' that accepts two parameters, compares them with both == and ===, and returns an object containing both comparison results.

steps.title: Execute the main function and log results
steps.instruction: Call the typeCoercionDemo function and use console.log to display the results of all your type coercion, equality, and truthy/falsy examples.
steps.hint: Add a function call to typeCoercionDemo() at the end of your file, after the function definitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: The typeCoercionDemo function will be called, executing all the code inside it and logging the results to the console.
successCriteria: typeCoercionDemo is called with parentheses () to execute the function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're calling the function with parentheses: typeCoercionDemo().
steps.feedbackWrong: The function call is missing. Add typeCoercionDemo() at the end of your file to execute all the demonstrations.
